method: Each row is a published claim that a quantum device did something a classical computer could not, in the claimants' own words, and every classical response we could find in journals and on arXiv. Dates are the first public posting of each paper (the arXiv version where there is one, otherwise the journal date). A response counts toward 'days to a classical answer' only if it targets the same experiment and its authors say they ran it. The status is the desk's reading of those responses, not a verdict from either side.

statuses.matched: A published classical method reproduces or beats the experiment's reported benchmark, by its own authors' account.
statuses.contested: Classical work claims to match the result at some scales, on some instances, or for a later experiment in the same line, and the dispute is not closed.
statuses.standing: We found no published classical reproduction as of the check date. This is an absence in our search, not a proof.

claim.label: Arute et al., Nature 574, 505
claim.claimed: About 200 seconds to take a million samples, against an estimate of 10,000 years on a classical supercomputer.

responses.by: Pednault, Gunnels, Nannicini, Horesh and Wisnieff (IBM)
responses.label: arXiv:1910.09534
responses.what: Argued that such circuits can be simulated on the Summit supercomputer in a matter of days. An argument about cost, not a run. Posted two days before the Nature paper, after the 2019 leak.

responses.label: arXiv:2103.03074
responses.what: One million correlated bitstrings at a cross-entropy score of 0.739 on 60 GPUs. Correlated samples, so not the same task as the experiment's uncorrelated ones.

responses.label: arXiv:2110.14502
responses.what: Sycamore sampling in 304 seconds on the new Sunway supercomputer (SC21). Correlated samples, so not the same task as the experiment's uncorrelated ones.

responses.label: arXiv:2111.03011; Physical Review Letters 129, 090502 (2022)
responses.what: One million uncorrelated bitstrings at a fidelity of about 0.0037 in about 15 hours on a cluster of 512 GPUs. The first run with uncorrelated samples at a fidelity above Google's.

responses.by: Zhao, Zhong, F. Pan, P. Zhang, J.-W. Pan, Chen and co-authors
responses.label: arXiv:2406.18889; National Science Review 12, nwae317
responses.what: 1,432 GPUs; a higher linear cross-entropy score than the experiment and, by the authors' account, seven times faster than Sycamore's run.

rows.reason: Two papers, with overlapping authors (Feng Pan and Pan Zhang appear on both), report running classical samplers that reach or exceed the experiment's score. The 10,000-year estimate did not survive; the experiment itself is not in doubt.

rows.task: Gaussian boson sampling, up to 76 photon clicks (Jiuzhang)

claim.label: Zhong et al., Science 370, 1460
claim.claimed: A sampling rate about 10^14 times faster than the best known classical simulation on supercomputers.

responses.label: arXiv:2108.01622; Science Advances 8, eabl9236 (2022)
responses.what: Cuts the estimated cost of classically simulating state-of-the-art Gaussian boson sampling, Jiuzhang scale included (up to 100 modes, 92 photons), from 600 million years to months on a supercomputer of about 100,000 cores. A cost estimate, not a run.

responses.label: arXiv:2109.11525
responses.what: Names the 2020 and 2021 experiments and gives classical samplers with better total variation distance and KL divergence than the experiments, by the authors' account. The benchmark is low-order marginals, which the USTC authors dispute as a test.
responses.table_note: a sampler that beats the experiment on distance measures, not a full simulation

responses.by: Oh, Liu, Alexeev, Fefferman and Jiang
responses.label: arXiv:2306.03709; Nature Physics 20, 1461 (2024)
responses.what: A tensor-network sampler that, they report, simulates the ideal distribution better than the experiment does, for the largest Gaussian boson sampling experiment so far. The abstract does not name which experiment, so we do not count it as an answer to the 2020 one.

rows.reason: Two classical papers target the 2020 and 2021 experiments: a cost estimate in months rather than millions of years, and a sampler that beats the experiments on distance measures. Whether those measures are the right test is disputed, so the line stays contested. A later classical sampler (Oh et al.) beats the largest experiment of its day on the authors' own measure; whether it answers this one is not stated in the paper. The 255-click Jiuzhang 3.0 (arXiv:2304.12240) and the 8,176-mode 2026 Nature experiment are separate claims and are not on this list.

rows.task: Kicked Ising dynamics on a 127-qubit processor, error-mitigated
rows.kind: 'utility' claim (IBM's own word; not called advantage)

claim.label: Kim et al., Nature 618, 500
claim.claimed: Accurate expectation values from a noisy 127-qubit processor, beyond the reach of the brute-force classical methods of the day.

responses.label: arXiv:2306.14887; PRX Quantum 5, 010308 (2024)
responses.what: Tensor networks with belief propagation, reported as significantly more accurate and precise than the experiment, and able to reach the thermodynamic limit.

responses.label: arXiv:2306.16372
responses.what: Fast classical simulation by sparse Pauli dynamics of the same experiment.

responses.label: arXiv:2306.15970
responses.what: Google's own classical analysis of the same experiment, a third attempt.

rows.reason: Two independent classical methods simulated the experiment within two weeks of the paper. IBM did not call it advantage; it is on this list because it was widely read as one.

claim.label: Morvan et al., arXiv:2304.11119; Nature 634, 328 (October 2024)
claim.claimed: Beyond the reach of existing classical supercomputers at this size. The arXiv version, posted April 2023, already carried the 67-qubit claim.

responses.by: Aharonov, Gao, Landau, Liu and Vazirani
responses.label: arXiv:2211.03999; STOC 2023
responses.what: A polynomial-time classical algorithm for noisy random circuit sampling at a constant noise rate per gate. Its authors say it is not practical in its present form and does not address finite-size experiments. It predates the claim, so it is context, not a response.

rows.reason: We found no published classical reproduction of this experiment's samples. The one general result (above) is asymptotic and its authors say it does not cover experiments of this size. Google's December 2024 Willow post gives a figure of under five minutes against 10^25 years; that belongs to a separate 105-qubit experiment on a different chip and is not what this row tests. A classical-cost figure of that size is a model estimate, and the 2019 estimate fell, so it is not a safe number.

rows.task: Quantum annealing dynamics of spin glasses
rows.kind: beyond-classical claim (D-Wave's press release said 'quantum supremacy')

claim.label: King et al., arXiv:2403.00910; Science 388, 199 (2025)
claim.claimed: Annealing processors generate samples in close agreement with the Schrödinger equation faster than leading classical methods (tensor networks and neural networks).

responses.by: Tindall, Mello, Fishman, Stoudenmire and Sels (Flatiron Institute)
responses.label: arXiv:2503.05693; Science 392, 868 (2026)
responses.what: Tensor networks with belief propagation; the authors report state-of-the-art accuracy with modest computational resources, on the same spin-glass models. Published in Science, May 2026.

responses.label: arXiv:2503.08247
responses.what: A time-dependent variational Monte Carlo method matching or beating D-Wave's reported accuracy on systems up to 128 spins; not shown at D-Wave's largest instances.

rows.reason: Two classical groups say they match the result, one on the experiment's own instances, one at smaller sizes. D-Wave's largest instances are not claimed by the second. One is now in a journal (Science, May 2026); neither has settled the question.

claim.label: Google Research post; Nature, 'Observation of constructive interference at the edge of quantum ergodicity'
claim.claimed: About two hours on Willow against an estimate of 13,000 times longer on a classical supercomputer.

responses.by: Bermejo, Villalonga, Ware, Vidal and Szasz
responses.label: arXiv:2604.15427
responses.what: Argues that tensor networks with belief propagation cannot feasibly simulate the experiment. This supports the claim against one named method. All five authors list Google Quantum AI as an affiliation (Bermejo also lists two Spanish institutions), so it is not an independent test.

rows.reason: No published classical simulation found. Google's own post says its team spent an estimated ten person-years red-teaming the result with nine classical algorithms; that is the claimant's account.

rows.task: Floquet dynamics on up to 74 qubits (IBM Heron with Qedma error suppression)

claim.label: IBM newsroom announcement
claim.claimed: Quantum advantage on commercially available hardware, in a pre-print that is not yet peer reviewed. IBM and Qedma say classical methods could not consistently agree at the scale reached and that the result was cross-validated on Quantinuum trapped-ion hardware. The circuits are released to the Quantum Advantage Tracker for classical benchmarking.

rows.reason: Announced 64 days before this check. The circuits are public for classical attempts and we have not recorded a published reproduction. IBM's own 2025 prediction, that the wider community would confirm a case by the end of 2026, is tracked on the Ledger.
